title: Xi’s Delhi visit: China’s new tone, old assumptions about India
gist: Xi's first India visit in seven years, at the New Delhi BRICS summit, brought partnership rhetoric, but the author argues China's historically dismissive view of India as a lesser rival persists beneath it, alongside a huge power gap, an unresolved border and a $100bn+ trade deficit.

insights.claim: Xi Jinping visited New Delhi for the BRICS summit, his first India trip in seven years, and told Modi the two countries should be partners rather than rivals.
insights.speaker: Saqlain Rizve
insights.so_what: Signals thaw in China-India ties, but rhetoric is not policy change.

insights.claim: Better leader-level relations do not necessarily change how each country views the other; China-India disputes over territory, influence and status persist.
insights.speaker: Saqlain Rizve
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate summit warmth into durable de-escalation or supply-chain integration.
insights.quote: But better relations do not necessarily mean a different view of each other.

insights.claim: The BRICS declaration repeated China's support for India playing a greater UN role including the Security Council, but this language is not new and stops short of endorsing a permanent Indian seat.
insights.speaker: Saqlain Rizve
insights.so_what: Treat as low-cost diplomacy rather than a concession on India's status.
insights.locator: The September summit offers a test

insights.claim: The border dispute is unresolved: the 2020 Galwan clash killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese by Beijing's count, a 2024 agreement eased the stand-off, yet troops remain deployed and boundary talks have made limited progress.
insights.speaker: Saqlain Rizve
insights.so_what: Residual military tail risk on the Himalayan frontier remains.

insights.claim: Bilateral trade hit a record $155.6 billion in 2025 per Chinese customs, with India importing about $132 billion of Chinese goods in FY2025-26 and running a deficit above $100 billion; India wants better market access and more dependable supply chains.
insights.speaker: Saqlain Rizve
insights.so_what: Trade dependence and India's access demands are the main economic bargaining chips; watch for market-access deals.

insights.claim: China's 2025 economy is about $19.5 trillion against nearly $4 trillion for India, and China's military spending of $336 billion dwarfs India's $92.1 billion.
insights.speaker: Saqlain Rizve
insights.so_what: The scale asymmetry underpins Beijing's reluctance to treat India as a peer.
insights.locator: The gap in overall power is also large

insights.claim: Political scientist Raj Verma argues China's dismissive view of India is shaped by history and cognitive bias, including early 20th-century Chinese intellectuals who saw colonised India as a warning and called it a wang guo, or lost country.
insights.speaker: Saqlain Rizve
insights.so_what: Perception-based drivers mean economic engagement alone may not change Beijing's strategic stance.

insights.claim: China's dismissive image of India was set when the economies were similar in size (about $150bn for China and $137bn for India in 1978), so the attitude predates the present economic gap.
insights.speaker: Saqlain Rizve
insights.so_what: Attitudes are sticky and not simply a function of relative GDP.

insights.claim: Manjeet Pardesi describes India as a lesser rival in Chinese strategic thinking that can still obstruct Beijing's ambitions in Asia, while China focuses mainly on the US and India sees China as its central security concern.
insights.speaker: Saqlain Rizve
insights.so_what: The rivalry is asymmetric: India prioritises China, China prioritises the US, shaping how much Beijing will concede.
insights.locator: Manjeet S. Pardesi reached a related conclusion

insights.claim: Xiaoyu Pu's 'ambivalent accommodation' reading holds that Beijing can welcome India as a developing-country partner while hesitating to accept its great-power claims, with recognition shifting with political interests.
insights.speaker: Saqlain Rizve
insights.so_what: Gives a more optimistic scenario in which recognition tracks the state of relations.
insights.locator: A third study offers a more optimistic reading
